answers.stem_only: Use an S3 event notification on object creation that invokes a Lambda function to build each thumbnail; serverless, scales with the bursty uploads, nothing to manage.
Lambda allocates CPU in proportion to the memory setting, so raise the memory setting; no code change needed.
Lambda concurrency quotas are per Region; request the same quota increase in the standby Region ahead of time and keep the two Regions' quotas in sync.
Switch to asynchronous invocation (Lambda queues the event and retries on failure) and configure an on-failure destination such as an SQS queue to keep events that still fail.

Attach the function to private subnets (with a security group allowed by the database) and route internet-bound traffic from those subnets through a NAT gateway in a public subnet; keep the database private.

Reuse the execution environment: load the file once in initialization code outside the handler and/or cache it in /tmp (ephemeral storage) so warm invocations do not download it again; staleness for the environment's lifetime is accepted.
Front the function with an API Gateway REST API: one API key per partner, usage plans with daily quotas, and an AWS WAF web ACL associated with the API stage.
Package the function as a container image (much larger size limit than .zip plus layers), push the image to an ECR repository in the same Region, and create the function from the image.
30 seconds per file fits well within the Lambda timeout: S3 event notification invokes a Lambda function that converts each file.
A Compute Savings Plan (three-year) covers EC2, Fargate and Lambda and stays flexible when workloads move between them.
The account-level Regional concurrency quota is the bottleneck; request a quota increase in Service Quotas sized for the peak.
Set reserved concurrency to 50 on the function; it caps the function at 50 concurrent executions with no architecture change.

answers.flag: A dead-letter queue (option B) also keeps the failed event with ErrorCode and ErrorMessage message attributes, so B with E is defensible unless the stem asks for something only a destination record gives (for example the response payload or full invocation context).
answers.stem_only: S3 invokes asynchronously: configure an on-failure destination (SQS queue) whose invocation record carries the event plus error details, and set maximum retry attempts to 0 so the failure is delivered right after the first attempt.
40 minutes exceeds the Lambda maximum timeout of 15 minutes; use an event-driven container task, for example EventBridge rule on S3 object created that runs an ECS task on Fargate per file.
For an SQS event source, configure a redrive policy with a dead-letter queue on the source SQS queue (maxReceiveCount), not a Lambda DLQ.
Put Amazon RDS Proxy in front of the DB instance to pool and share connections; point the functions at the proxy endpoint.
Configure provisioned concurrency (50) on a published version or alias and have API Gateway invoke that alias, so environments are pre-initialized.
Provisioned concurrency applies only to the qualified alias or version; point the API Gateway integration at the live alias ARN.
For high steady-state traffic, run the container on ECS with Fargate behind an ALB: no servers to manage and cheaper than per-request Lambda billing at constant high load.

On the Kinesis event source mapping, enable bisect batch on function error, set maximum retry attempts (and/or maximum record age), and add an on-failure destination (SQS or SNS) for the failed record metadata.
Orchestrate with an AWS Step Functions state machine: each Lambda function is a task with Retry and Catch rules, and the execution history shows each step.
Set reserved concurrency of 200 on the payment function so that this concurrency is set aside and other functions cannot use it.
